The research was conducted by Whittaker Corporation under USAF Contract F33615-71-C-1795 from July 1, 1971 to June 30, 1972.
The program was sponsored by the Air Force Materials Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio.
The target temperature range for the materials was ambient to 1600°F.
Aluminum phosphate (AlPO₄) can be used at temperatures up to 3000°F after curing to only 600°F.
The crystalline inversion in aluminum phosphate occurs at approximately 1140°F with a linear dimensional change of approximately 1.5%.
Lithium-aluminum-silicate additives successfully reduced thermal expansion and eliminated crystalline inversions.
Five ceramic matrix compositions were selected for further evaluation in Phase I.
The B-staging process involved heating at 150°F, 200°F, and 250°F for one hour each before ball milling.
Final curing of molded tiles was performed at up to 600°F for two hours.
Composite panels were 12 inches square and subjected to 165 dB acoustical vibration testing.
Mechanical property degradation at ambient temperature after 1600°F exposure occurred within one hour but then stabilized.
Extended aging at 1600°F for up to 200 hours had minimal effect on physical and electrical properties.
Silica fiber with amino silane finish and DC805 silicone resin size coating showed improved thermal stability.
The research addressed the 600°F temperature limitation of existing fiber-reinforced plastic-based RAM systems.
X-ray diffraction studies were performed to analyze crystallographic changes in candidate matrix materials.
Scanning electron microscope analysis was conducted on composite microstructures before and after 1600°F exposure.
Dielectric constant and loss tangent values were measured up to 1600°F at 8.52 GHz frequency.
Flexural strength and modulus were determined versus temperature before and after thermal aging.
